stories.title: R.K. Laxman's Bank Run
stories.description: Ajay recounts reading an R.K. Laxman novel as a child which gave him his first understanding of a bank run—how a queue of five people can turn into five hundred in no time, causing a bank to collapse.

stories.title: The 1993 Settlement Crisis
stories.description: Ajay describes the chaos when foreign investment first started flowing into India in 1993. The BSE's archaic settlement system choked, and truckloads of share certificates were seen on the streets of Bombay.

stories.title: NSDL Inauguration
stories.description: Ajay recalls one of the happiest days of his life, November 6, 1996, when the NSDL was inaugurated. Finance Minister P. Chidambaram hugged C.B. Bhave after pressing a button to simulate the first transaction.

stories.title: Mukesh Ambani's Driver
stories.description: Ajay shares a story told by Mukesh Ambani. In the past, his driver had to ask him for a loan. Recently, a teenager at Metro cinema asked Ambani, 'Do you want a loan?', illustrating the explosion of credit access in India.

stories.title: Deepak Parekh's Confession
stories.description: Ajay mentions that in the late 90s, Deepak Parekh of HDFC told him that in the entire history of HDFC, they had never repossessed a house, highlighting the lack of effective bankruptcy laws at the time.

Amit recommends this classic locked-room mystery by John Dickson Carr, using the 'melting ice cube' solution as a metaphor for bankruptcy.

recommendations.item: The Seen and the Unseen: Ajay Shah's Life and Times
recommendations.comment: Amit recommends the marathon 10.5-hour episode where they discuss Ajay's career and Indian finance in depth.

core_ideas.description: For decades, Indian banking was run as a central planning system (a form of taxation), which stifled innovation and risk-taking. It was a bureaucracy, not a market.
The creation of SEBI, NSE, and NSDL was a rare success where 'knowledge and community' came together to build world-class institutions, breaking the old clubby monopoly of the BSE.

A situation where individuals are rational and good, but the systemic outcome is broken and tragic (like the pre-reform stock market). It's a trap that's hard to escape without collective action or state intervention.
Ajay argues that systemic risk in India is often caused by domestic failures in monetary policy, regulation, and resolution, rather than just being imported from global crises.
India often creates institutions that look like Western ones (e.g., a bond market, an inflation-targeting central bank) but lack the internal capability and genuine function. It's a facade.

core_ideas.item: Bankruptcy as a Melting Ice Cube
core_ideas.description: A distressed firm loses value rapidly. Speed is crucial in bankruptcy proceedings to preserve the organizational capital (people, processes) before it melts away.
Restricting the movement of capital is a violation of human freedom, similar to restricting movement of people. It disproportionately hurts the poor, while the rich find ways around it.

jokes_and_cultural_references.context: Amit quotes Max Planck on how paradigms change.
Ajay jokes that RBI acts like a 'mother' who hides the bad news (bank failures) from the children (the public).
Ajay uses the metaphor of the central bank pouring LSD into the punch bowl to describe loose monetary policy fueling bubbles.
Amit jokes that he would rename FEMA to this.
Ajay quotes Miss Prism from 'The Importance of Being Earnest' calling the fall of the rupee 'too sensational'.
